newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Gold - Output, forward sales seen up.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Gold - Output, forward sales seen up.

text.p: Australian gold production is expected to increase as new mines are developed and existing ones expand, despite a strong likelihood that Australian-dollar gold prices are going down.
A rise in forward selling among Australian producers -- already the biggest forward sellers in the world -- should accompany the additional output, analysts said on Thursday.
Australia is on track to produce in excess of 300 tonnnes of gold in 1995/97 versus 272.9 tonnes in 1995/96.
It is estimated Australian producers currently have sold forward some 350 tonnes at various price levels, a figure that is seen rising.
A number of producers liquidated portions of their forward positions when gold lease rates increased earlier this year.
Whether the level of forward selling surpasses last year's figure of 530 tonnes is questionable, but few doubt the number is going up.
Australia and the United States lead the world in forward sales, although the strategy is holding increasing appeal for the world's biggest producer, South Africa.
In South Africa, spiralling mine operating costs, an increasing rand price and high interest rates all point to more forward selling

Simon Middleton of the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) estimates seven percent of Australia's gold mines currently operate at costs above a projected 1995/96 gold price of A$514 an ounce, which means they are being kept afloat by hedging future output at a higher price.
"A lot of these producers are forward selling 10 to 20 percent above the spot price," Middleton said.

Moreover, forward sales are tipped to increase as some miners who drew down their positions when gold lease rates soared to around six or seven percent earlier this year reinstate their positions now that the rates have retreated.
Middleton expects gold to average only A$487 an ounce in 1996/97, a 5.3 percent decline year-on-year.

He agrees with other analysts that mine supply next year will outstrip demand from the fabricating industries, seen growing at around three percent annually, and that inflation will be of little concern to potential investors.
These factors should lead to lower prices, in turn encouraging more forward selling.
